display_title: Official Review of Paper1241 by Reviewer 7awx

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a method for fast and memory efficient cross-modal indexing based on mapping of the queries to a predefined set of items. The method is tested on several small-scale datasets and compared to some other cross-model indexing methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Weaknesses:
1) The paper claims O(1) complexity of retrieval, which is better than a balanced tree on 1D data. While the algorithm technically might have that complexity by design, the practicality of using the algorithm at large sizes will likely suffer (e.g. the recall will drop to zero at an infinite size). The latter has not been discussed in the paper.
2) The paper uses tiny datasets, far from the sizes of existing datasets (why not test it on LAION-2B or similar datasets?)
3) The paper does not compare to the existing approximate nearest neighbor search methods applied to a transformer distance. Graph ANN algorithms can work with transformers as a matching function, so they can speed up the “single stream approach” while having the almost the same quality. E.g. [Tan, Shulong, et al. "Fast item ranking under neural network based measures." Proceedings of the 13th International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining. 2020; Morozov, Stanislav, and Artem Babenko. "Relevance Proximity Graphs for Fast Relevance Retrieval." arXiv preprint arXiv:1908.06887 (2019).]
4) The paper has strange estimates of memory. E.g. for the “single stream” method the memory consumption is assumed to be zero - this seems very unrealistic as the network inputs have to be stored somewhere.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
I think most of the aspects of the paper are not novel by itself, though combination of those at specific accuracy/latency/memory cost might be considered somewhat novel. 
Paper writing can be improved, e.g. "typically unsatisfied in accuracy" in the abstract.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper makes strange O(1) complexity claims for retrieval, tests only at small scale and does not have a comprehensive set of baselines. I think this it is below the bar for ICLR.
content.correctness: 1: The main claims of the paper are incorrect or not at all supported by theory or empirical results.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1241 by Reviewer sK5a

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: Authors propose a novel approach for cross-modal retrieval (text-to-image, image-to-text), that has strong accuracy despite very low memory and high speed at inference time. Authors propose novel hierarchical indexing strategy that is used to train encoder-decoder network that maps queries (image or text features) into a sequence of indices from the constructed hierarchical tree.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- This approach is clearly superior to related work wrt memory and speed at inference
- Accuracy is strong given the cost at inference time
- Approach is interesting and novel as far as I can tell. It differs significantly from related work, and the whole paradigm of using indexing/hashing in multi-modal embeddings (image and text embeddings concatenated) is very interesting and might result in a new line of research

Weaknesses:
- My major weakness is in experimental section, as I dont see is strong enough to showcase the benefits of the approach. I will be more detailed in the following:
  - There is no baseline. Authors use CLIP model features, so an obvious baseline would be directly using features from CLIP for retrieval via cosine similarity (corresponds to (b) in Fig 2). Also, implementation details are missing some key information (I am sorry if I did not see it). Eg, what is the architecture of ViT, is it B/16 or L/14 or something else? Looking at CLIP results on Flickr i2t 88.0 and t2i 68.7, seems like vanilla zero-shot CLIP is much better than this approach, while being much simpler, ie not requiring additional training steps and modeling? Additionally one could do approx NN or PCA-dimensionality reduction as very straghtforward baselines on top of CLIP, which reduce memory and increase speed with minor accuracy reduction.
  - Comparison with related work in Tables 1 and 4 is quite flawed: (i) COCO is a more representative dataset as it is bigger, so why is it in suppl? Makes it hard to jump forward and backward to compare. In fact, authors could merge Tabs 1 and 4 and report only r@1 (I personally believe r@5 can fit as well), and do two tables for missing r@5 and r@10 numbers in suppl. (ii) It is unclear what are architectures of related works, are they all based on CLIP features like this method (can we have a table where only CLIP-embeddings based methods are compared), what are datasets used to pretrain, and train additional encoder-decoder transformers or cross/co-attention transformers, what are feature dimensionalities, etc. It is hard to compare approaches in this way apples-to-apples. (iii) How does this method, or others, hold up against increasing database/gallery size, ie do they only work well because COCO and Flickr databases are small? What about constructing the evaluation over an increasing database size as x-axis of a plot?
- Method is quite complex, requires different phases in training, versus (a) (b) and (c) which are quite simple. Not sure how would this approach scale with this complexity of implementation and many moving parts and design choices.
- So minor issues:
  - Fig 2(d) is a bit unclear, seems like identifier memory is not used in fact, arrows directions are not clear to me. 
  - Retrieval accuracy is not comparable with SOTA as claimed on several places around paper, seems to be quite far from single-stream SOTA. I do understand this is a paper about speed and memory efficiency, but one should be clear when presenting.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Paper was easy to read, even with the complex method I managed to understand key components
- Approach is novel, see strengths
- There are issues around experimental quality of the paper, see weaknesses
- There are issues with reproducibility of the pipeline, see weaknesses, I think it is very complex and potentially over-fitted to small datasets used at eval. Not sure how would one scale this to billion-scale, where hashing methods are mostly popular and important.
content.summary_of_the_review: Approach is novel and interesting, but I have strong concerns around experimental presentation and understanding how the method performs in an apple-to-apple comparison. Also, there is no single baseline, even though authors build on top of a popular CLIP model, that can be used for the same task. Finally, I have issues around approach complexity and its scalability to extremely large dataset, there is no signal that such an approach would not break at billion scale, even though this is where memory and speed issues are of biggest concern.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to tackle three problems in cross-modal retrieval, i.e., effectiveness, efficiency, and memory. A cross-modal indexing algorithm is built to jointly consider the above three factors. Experiments validate their claims on cross-modal retrieval.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
There are some strengths of this paper:
The proposed method seems to well balance the high accuracy, fast speed, and low storage in cross-modal retrieval.
A new method of cross-modal indexing is built to make fast and accurate retrieval.
Experiments on several datasets show the effectiveness of the proposed method by comparing it to some sota algorithms.

The weakness of the paper is also clear:
1. Generally, the reviewer believes this paper is irrelevant to representation learning but database, while it is the main theme of ICLR. But, if you argue using some deep learning or cross-media intelligence techniques for retrieval tasks, the reviewer may not agree.
2. Three key points shown in this paper are more like a project, rather than technical contributions, although some researchers think research should be more related to practical systems. But, it is not always right.
1) Building an index tree with hierarchical clustering is a general trick in file indexing systems, and also simply appears in database systems.
2) Index learning is built on encoder-decoder formulation, while it is hard to make sufficient cross-modal interaction which is the key to cross-modal retrieval.
3) The index sampling proposed is built on the well-known beam search with modification.
3. For experiments, indexing is always used for big data. In Table 1, if you think the gray works are not useful for comparison, why did you add them to the table?
4. It is known that there is no free lunch. For machine learning algorithms, it is really impossible to jointly consider these three parts. To me, there are lots of pre-defined processes, but are there any weaknesses?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The overall idea of this paper is good and the novelty of this paper is clear. Moreover, the motivation, strength, and objective are easy to figure out. However, it is hard to make reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper is well-written and easy to follow, but the overall algorithm or settings are very complex. THe topic of this paper is more related to the database field rather than ML or CV and even multimedia.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1241 by Reviewer PjEF

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a new framework for the cross-model retrieval problem that achieves fast inference speed, low storage requirement and (reasonably) high accuracy. The proposed model, the cross-modal indexing (CMI), generates hierarchical tree of all observed input-output pairs and therefore defines the sequential identifiers (SID) via the path from tree root to a leaf. Sequence generation models with shared decoder are trained so that relevant pairs are decoded into the same SID. Empirical results show that the proposed method has comparable accuracy as published baseline models while enjoys much faster inference speed and much lower memory consumption.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
* The model proposed in the paper combines a sequence generation model with the retrieval problem and therefore has much faster inference speed compared with brute-force search and higher accuracy compared with QP based ANN method.

Weaknesses
* There discussion of the cross-model retrieval paradigms has missed some important models. The CMH framework is the CME(two-stream) with ANN search accelerated by product quantization. Similarly, CME(two-stream) inference can be accelerated by graph based ANN search (e.x. HNSW), which is not covered in discussion nor the experiments.

* All the empirical results reported in the main text are on a single dataset Flicker30K. It would make the observation more convincing if the author can extend the experiments to other retrieval tasks and datasets.

* The memory calculation only includes the indexing or the label embedding but not the encoder networks. While retrieval problems with millions or billions of candidates the space taken by the encoder is negligible, this is not the case here as the largest problem in the experiment has only 30K candidates. For example, a 12-layer transformer model  has 300M parameters, much larger than 30K * 1024 (number of parameters in candidate embeddings).

* It is also not clear how the framework would scale to large scale retrieval problems, especially when the SID requires generating hierarchical tree on all observed training pairs. The number of observed pairs is orders of magnitudes larger than the number of candidate documents in a retrieval problem, and generating reasonably good hierarchical trees on billions of items is not a trivial task.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

* It is still not clear to me how the ID gallery is defined and how it is constructed given the hierarchical tree. Could you give a formal definition and more explanation here?

* If the inference is done through beam search, why is its time complexity O(1) rather than the depth of the tree (O(log(n)))?

**Quality**
Overall the paper is well structured, however there are some minor issues such as abusing notations (N stands for both bath-size and search space size, coding length can be T/M/W).


**Reproducibility**
The experimental settings are described in detail and should be enough for reproduce. Although it would be better if the authors plan to share their code.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work proposes a method to encode all observed input-output pairs in a retrieval problem via paths in a hierarchical tree and adopts a sequence generation model with beam search for retrieving. Whereas the idea is novel and the model does enjoy fast inference speed and low memory consumption, experiments are only conducted on very limited application scenarios and dataset. Also, some of the claims made in the paper have minor issue or not well supported. Overall I think this is an interesting direction worth exploring but the current condition of the paper does not meet the bar for this venue.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
